changes.before: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Korean Minnesotans include immigrant families and their U.S.-born children, and Korean adoptees, most of whom were raised by non-Korean families. Most of the research below is about immigrant families and may not apply to adoptees at all. We found no Minnesota study of Korean families and disability. Two Minnesota-relevant figures are not disability studies as such. A University of Minnesota study (Keyes et al., 2008) assessed 514 international adoptees, most born in South Korea per NPR's report, alongside domestic adoptees and nonadopted teens in Minnesota. It found most adopted teens psychologically healthy, with roughly double the odds of contact with a mental health professional and of a disruptive behavior disorder. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports a Korean disability rate of 5.5 percent, and 5.0 percent under age 65. The studies are few, small, set mainly in Los Angeles or New York, and in some cases available only in summary.
